960.title: Ain Jalut, 1260
960.hook: the Mamluks of Egypt stop the Mongol advance in Palestine
960.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Talut and Jalut in surah al-Baqarah, and its line that Allah is with the steadfast is often quoted in times of hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Baghdad, sacked, and a river the chronicles say ran dark with ink. Your line was the river of ink.

A letter arrives in Cairo from the Mongol camp. The chronicles say it demands surrender, with threats to match. Baghdad has fallen. The cities of Syria have fallen or opened their gates. The sultan of Egypt, a soldier named Qutuz, has to answer. He could pay. He could wait behind the walls and hope. Instead, the chronicles say, he marches his army north, out of Egypt, to meet them. The two armies come face to face beside a spring in Palestine, with a name out of an old story. Today: Ain Jalut.
screen: `A LETTER DEMANDING SURRENDER.` → `QUTUZ MARCHES NORTH.` → `A SPRING WITH AN OLD NAME.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. 'Ayn is Arabic for a spring, and also for an eye. Jalut is the Qur'an's name for Goliath. So Ain Jalut is the spring of Goliath. The Qur'an tells that story in surah al-Baqarah. A king called Talut, often identified with Saul, leads an army out against Jalut. He tests his men at a river: whoever drinks from it isn't with me, except one who scoops up a single handful. Most of them drink. Only a few hold back. And that small group, facing Jalut's army, says, in Pickthall's English: "How many a little company hath overcome a mighty host by Allah's leave! Allah is with the steadfast." They ask Allah for patience and firm feet. Then, the Qur'an says, David killed Goliath. Now the battle. The Mamluk army met the Mongols at that spring, and the Mamluks won. The Mongol advance toward Egypt stopped there. Among Qutuz's commanders was a man named Baybars. And history doesn't end tidily: on the way home, the chronicles say, Qutuz was killed by his own officers, and Baybars became sultan. Why does the name matter? Because, for the people who told this story, the place seemed to speak: a spring named for Goliath, where an army that had seemed unstoppable was stopped. In this story, Allah is with the steadfast, the ones who hold their ground. Holding your ground isn't the same as winning every fight. It means there's a line, and you stay on it.

961.title: The Mongols become Muslim
961.hook: within decades, Mongol rulers in Persia embrace Islam
961.howItsDone: Muslims tell the conversion of the Mongol rulers as a story of hearts turned, and the Prophet's prayer to the turner of hearts, asking for a heart kept firm in faith, is still said by Muslims today.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ain Jalut, where the Mamluks stopped the Mongol advance beside a spring named for Goliath. Your line was the spring of goliath.

A Mongol prince stands before a gathering and takes a new name: Mahmud. Until then his name was Ghazan. He is a descendant of Chinggis Khan, reaching for the throne of Persia, the land his family's armies once overran. Rashid al-Din, who would serve him as vizier and write the history of the Mongols, describes him as raised a Buddhist. And now he declares himself a Muslim. Same family, same throne: an heir of the storm from the east, praying toward Mecca. Today: the Mongols become Muslim.
screen: `A PRINCE TAKES A NEW NAME.` → `GHAZAN BECOMES MAHMUD.` → `THE STORM'S HEIR PRAYS.`

segments.voice: It wasn't only Ghazan. In the north, Berke, khan of the Golden Horde, had become Muslim before him. In Persia, after Ghazan, the Mongol rulers were Muslims who built mosques, endowed schools and gave scholars their patronage. The family whose armies had sacked Baghdad now ruled as Muslim kings. The conquerors converted: the people who won the war took up the faith of the people they had defeated. Why? Historians weigh it differently. Some stress faith, the plain story Rashid al-Din tells of a ruler who came to believe. Some stress politics: a king ruling a land full of mosques does well to pray in them. Some point to the scholars, Sufis and ordinary people around the court, whose lives showed the conquerors what Islam looked like. Probably more than one of these at once. People are like that. And here's how the tradition itself talks about a change of heart. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that the hearts of people are between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful, and He turns them as He wills. Another report says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ often prayed, asking the turner of hearts to keep his heart firm. Some tell this story as a reminder that no one's ending is known in advance.

962.title: Al-Tusi's observatory
962.hook: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi builds an observatory at Maragha under Mongol rule
962.howItsDone: Muslims use the sky to set the times of prayer, the direction of Mecca and the months of the lunar calendar, and the sighting of the new moon marks the start and end of Ramadan for communities that follow local sighting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mongols become Muslim, and Ghazan takes the name Mahmud. Your line was the conquerors converted.

On a hilltop above the town of Maragha, in Persia, workmen are laying stone for a building whose whole purpose is to watch the sky. Inside will go great instruments for measuring where the stars and planets stand, and a library beside them. The money comes from Hulagu, the same Mongol prince whose army sacked Baghdad. The man in charge is a Persian scholar, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. The storm that, the chroniclers say, drowned books in a river is now paying for star charts. Today: al-Tusi's observatory.
screen: `A HILLTOP ABOVE MARAGHA.` → `INSTRUMENTS AND A LIBRARY.` → `PAID FOR BY HULAGU.`

segments.voice: Al-Tusi was a scholar of many fields: astronomy, mathematics, philosophy, ethics, and the theology of the Shia tradition he belonged to. He came into Hulagu's service and persuaded the prince to build the observatory at Maragha. They watched the sky night after night and wrote tables of where the heavens moved, tables astronomers went on using. Al-Tusi also worked on a hard problem from the Greek astronomy he had inherited: how to explain the planets' motions using only circles turning evenly. His answer is now called the Tusi couple. Picture a small circle rolling inside a bigger one, twice as wide. A point on the small circle doesn't go round and round. It goes straight back and forth, in a line. Some historians have noticed a very similar device in Copernicus's work, much later, and still debate how it got there. So, learning survived. Not untouched, not without cost. But the habit of looking up and measuring carefully didn't die with Baghdad. It moved to a hilltop and kept going. Why would a believer care about star tables? Partly for prayer: the times of prayer and the direction of Mecca are worked out from the sky. And partly because the Qur'an keeps pointing up. In surah Al 'Imran, in Pickthall's English: "Lo! In the creation of the heavens and the earth and (in) the difference of night and day are tokens (of His sovereignty) for men of understanding." For al-Tusi's circle, measuring the sky was one way of reading those tokens.
screen: `A SCHOLAR OF MANY FIELDS.` · `TABLES OF THE MOVING HEAVENS.` · `THE TUSI COUPLE: CIRCLES MAKE A LINE.` · `TOKENS FOR MEN OF UNDERSTANDING.` · then, large: `LEARNING SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: Look at the sky: step outside or go to a window, or, if you can't, close your eyes and remember the last night sky you really saw. 963.title: Mamluk Cairo
963.hook: former slave-soldiers rule Egypt and build mosques, hospitals and schools
963.howItsDone: Muslims speak of sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity, and some give to build or keep up mosques, schools, wells and hospitals in the hope that the good continues after them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Tusi's observatory on a hilltop at Maragha, paid for by a Mongol prince. Your line was learning survived.

A boy is sold in a market far from home, somewhere on the grasslands north of the Black Sea, and shipped to Egypt. There he is taught Arabic, the Qur'an and prayer, then the horse, the bow and the lance. When his training ends, he is freed and becomes a soldier of the sultan. That was the path of the mamluks. Some who walked it became sultans themselves, ruling Egypt from the citadel above Cairo. And then they started to build. Today: Mamluk Cairo.
screen: `A BOY SOLD FAR FROM HOME.` → `TRAINED, THEN FREED.` → `SOME BECAME SULTANS.`

segments.voice: In Arabic, mamluk means one who is owned. These were children bought and taken from their families. Nothing in today's story makes that good. What the story shows is what some of them did once they held power. They built. Walk down the old main street of Cairo today and their buildings still stand shoulder to shoulder: mosques, schools, fountains, tombs. Sultan Qalawun, once a mamluk himself, built a complex with his tomb, a school and a hospital, a bimaristan, side by side. The endowment that paid for the hospital, as historians describe it, was meant for anyone who was sick, rich or poor, man or woman, without charge. Later, his grandson Sultan Hasan, born a prince rather than bought, built a great mosque and college, with space for teaching the different schools of Sunni law under one roof. Why build like this? Partly for memory and standing, like rulers anywhere. But there's a teaching underneath, taught in the very schools they built. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end, except three: a charity that keeps on giving, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. A hospital is a charity that keeps on giving. A school is knowledge still in use. Men who had once been owned, and their heirs, may well have been thinking about what they would leave behind when they owned nothing again. Slaves became builders. People still pray in some of those mosques.
screen: `MAMLUK — ONE WHO IS OWNED.` · `QALAWUN: A TOMB, A SCHOOL, A HOSPITAL.` · `SULTAN HASAN'S MOSQUE AND COLLEGE.` · `THREE DEEDS THAT DON'T END.` · then, large: `SLAVES BECAME BUILDERS.`

If you pray, ask that whatever good it still does keep going; if not, simply hold it in mind.

964.title: Ibn Taymiyyah
964.hook: a Damascus scholar of the Mongol age, influential and debated, who called for return to early sources
964.howItsDone: Students of Islamic law and theology read Ibn Taymiyyah's fatwas and treatises alongside those of scholars who disagreed with him, and teachers stress reading each ruling with the question and setting that produced it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mamluk Cairo, where men who had once been owned built hospitals and schools. Your line was slaves became builders.

A question arrives at a scholar's door in Damascus. It concerns a town called Mardin. Its people are Muslims, but the power over them now belongs to the Mongols, whose armies have been raiding toward Syria. So which is it: a land of peace, or a land of war? The answer decides how people there are to be treated, and what they owe. The scholar gives an answer that fits neither box, and readers have argued over it ever since. Today: Ibn Taymiyyah.
screen: `A QUESTION ABOUT MARDIN.` → `PEACE OR WAR?` → `AN ANSWER STILL ARGUED OVER.`

segments.voice: Ibn Taymiyyah taught in Damascus in the age of the Mongol raids, a scholar of the Hanbali school, sharp, prolific, and not one to avoid a fight. His great call was to go back to the sources: the Qur'an, the Sunnah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the way of the earliest generations of Muslims, the salaf. Back past the layers, to the beginning. His answer on Mardin shows the kind of distinction he drew. The town, he said, was neither simply a land of peace nor simply a land of war, but a third kind, a mixture. The Muslims there were to be treated as Muslims, and those who had left the path as their conduct deserved. The question offered two colors, and he refused to paint with only two. His life was not quiet. He clashed with rulers and with other scholars, and was imprisoned more than once; his student Ibn Kathir records that he died a prisoner in the citadel of Damascus. His name is still argued over. Some Muslims call him Shaykh al-Islam and read him closely. Others, including theologians and Sufis, have disagreed with him sharply on important points. And in modern times his words have been quoted for very different purposes, sometimes cut loose from their questions. Hence today's line: read him in his age. A ruling written for a town under Mongol power, by a man watching armies on the border, has to be read with that town and those armies in view. That's true of any scholar. Know the question before you judge the answer.

965.title: The first refuge was Africa
965.hook: the first Muslim refugees were welcomed in Abyssinia
965.howItsDone: Muslims tell the emigration to Abyssinia as the first hijrah, and the Negus's protection of the refugees is remembered in sermons and lessons about sheltering the persecuted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Taymiyyah and his answer about Mardin: not peace, not war, a third kind. Your line was read him in his age.

Umar ibn al-Khattab walks into his daughter Hafsah's house in Medina and finds a visitor, a woman just back from across the sea: Asma bint Umays. When he learns where she has been, he tells her: we emigrated before you did, so we have more right to the Messenger of Allah than you. Asma doesn't laugh. She's angry. She says she won't eat or drink until she has taken it to the Prophet ﷺ himself. Where had she been? Today: the first refuge was Africa.
screen: `UMAR TEASES A VISITOR.` → `WE EMIGRATED BEFORE YOU.` → `ASMA TAKES IT TO THE PROPHET.`

segments.voice: Asma had been in Abyssinia, across the Red Sea in East Africa. Years earlier, in Mecca, believers who were being persecuted had crossed that sea, and a Christian king, the Negus, had sheltered them. Asma and her husband Ja'far were among them. Before there was a Medina to go to, there was Africa. Here's what she says back to Umar, as Sahih al-Bukhari reports it, in paraphrase. You were with the Prophet. He fed your hungry and taught your ignorant. We were far away, among strangers, in a land where we were hated, all of it for the sake of Allah and His Messenger. So she goes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and tells him what Umar said. And he answers: Umar has no more right to me than you do. He and his companions made one hijrah. You, the people of the ship, made two. One across the sea to Africa, and one from Africa to Medina. The Prophet counts the African years as a hijrah in their own right, not a detour. And the report adds one more detail. Abu Musa, who sailed home with them, says the people of the ship came to Asma in groups to hear her tell it, and nothing in the world made them happier or meant more to them than what the Prophet had said. That's where the story of Islam in Africa begins: not with an army, but with refugees and a king who would not hand them over.

966.title: Egypt and the Nile
966.hook: Amr ibn al-As enters Egypt in 640, and over centuries Egypt becomes mostly Muslim
966.howItsDone: Muslims in Egypt pray in mosques old and new, including the mosque of Amr ibn al-As in Cairo, and live alongside Coptic Christian neighbors whose churches go back to before Islam.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the people of the ship, and the Prophet's word that they had made two hijrahs. Your line was africa sheltered them first.

Remember the envoys from Mecca who sailed to Abyssinia with gifts for the Negus, hoping he'd hand the refugees back? Ibn Ishaq names one of them: Amr ibn al-As. He went home empty-handed. Later he became a Muslim himself, and a commander. And one day, under the caliph Umar, he leads an army west out of Palestine, across the edge of the desert, toward a green river valley that had been home to kings, temples and churches long before. Today: Egypt and the Nile.
screen: `AN ENVOY TO THE NEGUS.` → `NOW A MUSLIM COMMANDER.` → `WEST, TOWARD THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Egypt in Arabic is Misr, the name the Qur'an uses in the story of Yusuf, where Egypt is the land that takes him in, and where, in the end, his whole family comes to live. When Amr's army arrived, Egypt was ruled from Constantinople, and in its towns and villages the Arab soldiers met Coptic Christians. Amr took the fortress beside the Nile, and later Alexandria by the sea. Then he founded a new town on the river bank, Fustat, and built a mosque there. Rebuilt again and again, it still carries his name. Before any of this, a hadith in Sahih Muslim says, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his companions they would one day enter Egypt, and asked them to treat its people well, because they had a claim of protection and of kinship. Scholars explain the kinship through Hajar, the mother of Ismail, and through Mariyah the Copt, the mother of the Prophet's son Ibrahim. Now the part that's easy to get wrong. Egypt did not become Muslim when Amr arrived. Historians describe a slow change. Over generations, more and more Egyptians became Muslim, through marriage, through trade, through the pull of the cities, through taxes and law, through faith. Arabic slowly became the language of the street. And Coptic Christians stayed. They are still there, in their churches, and the old Coptic language is still sung in their liturgy. A country's faith didn't change in a battle. It changed in kitchens and markets, one family at a time, across lifetimes.
screen: `MISR — THE LAND THAT TOOK YUSUF IN.` · `AMR, FUSTAT, AND A MOSQUE.` · `TREAT ITS PEOPLE WELL: PROTECTION AND KINSHIP.` · `COPTS STAYED, AND STILL SING.` · then, large: `SLOWLY, OVER CENTURIES.`

segments.voice: Picture the mosque of Amr ibn al-As in old Cairo: a broad open courtyard under the sky, rows of columns holding up the roof, the noise of the city outside its walls. Rebuilt again and again and still in use, it has been prayed in by generations who each added a little. If you pray, make a dua for the people who pray there now; if not, simply hold the place in mind.
Misr. The Qur'an's name for Egypt, the land of Yusuf, which Amr ibn al-As entered, and where, slowly, families became Muslim beside Coptic neighbors. Today's word.
Your line: slowly, over centuries. The Copts are still there, still singing. Day nine hundred sixty-six, done.
